name: Slimming creams and lotions

lead: Slimming creams are topical products that claim to reduce fat or the dimpled look of cellulite where they are rubbed in, most often on thighs, hips, stomach and upper arms. Common active ingredients include caffeine and other xanthines, plant extracts such as green tea, guggul and ginseng, and oils. The appearance payoff users want is smoother, firmer-looking skin and slightly smaller measurements.

Published studies are small. A 2015 study of 15 people using a 3.5 percent caffeine and xanthine cream for six weeks reported a visual cellulite score improvement and thigh and arm circumference reductions of about 0.7 to 0.8 cm. A 2011 randomized split-body trial found a slimming cream added benefit on top of dietary advice.

paras: Users apply the cream to the target area, commonly twice a day, often with massage, over several weeks. Trials pair creams with diet advice, and some creams are used with massage tools or wraps.

Slight itching and transient flushing were common in the caffeine cream study, with no serious events. Case reports describe allergic contact dermatitis to an ingredient (guggul) in a slimming cream. Dermatology sources describe cellulite as a normal condition that can be resistant to treatment.

angle.text: People apply slimming creams to areas where they want smoother or slimmer-looking skin. In trials, changes were measured in fractions of a centimetre and visual scores.

lead: Slimming creams and lotions are topical products sold to reduce localised fat, lessen the dimpled appearance of cellulite and firm skin on areas such as thighs, hips and upper arms. The appearance goal is smaller measurements and smoother-looking skin where the cream is applied [1][2].

Typical formulas combine caffeine or other xanthines with plant extracts, oils and moisturisers; patents describe creams built on evening primrose oil, green tea and caffeine, ginsenoside and similar mixtures [3][4]. Companies position them as promoting lipolysis (fat breakdown) in the layer under the skin [2][5].

Human data come from small trials. A randomized right-left comparison reported extra improvement in cellulite score and thigh circumference on the treated side when combined with dietary advice [1], and a 2015 uncontrolled study of a caffeine cream reported small circumference reductions [2]. Wikipedia notes that cellulite can resist many treatments and that medical opinion often regards it as a normal condition [6].
infobox: Caffeine, xanthines, guggul, green tea, ginsenosides, evening primrose oil [2][3][4]

paras: Slimming creams come as creams, gels and lotions meant to be massaged in. Patents describe formulations including caffeine and green tea [4], evening primrose oil with herbs [3], and ginsenoside with peppermint oil [7]. Their stated aim is to burn or reduce subcutaneous fat or improve skin firmness.

A randomized controlled right/left trial in International Journal of Cosmetic Science (2011) gave participants dietary advice not based on calorie restriction and applied a slimming cream to one thigh and hip while the other served as control. Cellulite scores improved after 4 weeks on both sides, with greater and earlier improvement on the treated side, and the treated side also showed greater thigh circumference reduction and improved skin tonicity after 2 weeks [1].

A 2015 study in Annals of Dermatology gave 15 people a cream containing 3.5 percent water-soluble caffeine and xanthines to use twice daily for 6 weeks. The visual scale score improved by 19.8 percent, and thigh and upper-arm circumferences fell by 0.7 cm (1.7 percent) and 0.8 cm (2.3 percent); slight itching and transient flushing were common, with no serious adverse events. The authors called for larger trials [2].

An animal study in guinea pigs tested a slimming cream with a novel fabric intended to improve delivery into skin and reported thinner fat layers with that fabric, a laboratory finding rather than a human result [5].
Mild itching and flushing were reported in the caffeine cream study [2]. A 2007 case report in Contact Dermatitis described allergic contact dermatitis to guggul in a slimming cream [8].

Wikipedia's cellulite article lists creams among topical treatments, notes that cellulite can be resistant to treatment and that prevailing medical opinion treats it as a normal condition in many women [6].
